text: Manasseh Damukana Sogavare, born on 17 January 1955 in Popondetta, Northern Province, in the Territory of Papua (then part of the Australian-ruled Territory of Papua and New Guinea), is a Solomon Islander politician who served as prime minister of the Solomon Islands for a total of nine years, from 2000–2001, 2006–2007, 2014–2017, and 2019–2024. He has represented East Choiseul in the National Parliament since 1997 and served as minister of finance from 1997–1998, 2017–2019, and 2024–2025. Sogavare graduated with a bachelor’s degree in accounting and economics from the University of the South Pacific and a master’s degree in management studies from the University of Waikato in New Zealand. He previously held key positions including Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Finance (1994–1996), Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Director of the Central Bank of the Solomon Islands, and Chairman of the Solomon Islands National Provident Fund. He was first elected to Parliament in the 6 August 1997 election and became Minister of Finance and Treasury in 1997 under Prime Minister Bartholomew Ulufa'alu, though he was dismissed in mid-July 1998 without explanation, claiming the decision was made to maintain government stability. He withdrew support for Ulufa'alu, accusing him of authoritarianism, and later became deputy leader of the opposition in September 1998, then leader after Solomon Mamaloni's death in January 2000. Sogavare was elected prime minister on 30 June 2000 with 23 votes in favor and 21 against, following Ulufa'alu's resignation due to capture by rebels. He served until 17 December 2001. His party won only three seats in the 2001 election, but he remained in Parliament. In 2002 and again from 2005 to April 2006, he was a member of the Bills and Legislation Committee. After the 2006 general election, he led the Solomon Islands Social Credit Party into a coalition to oust Snyder Rini, receiving 11 of 50 votes to become prime minister on 18 April 2006, before switching support to Rini, who became prime minister and appointed Sogavare as Minister for Commerce, Industries and Employment. When Rini resigned on 26 April 2006, Sogavare won a parliamentary vote on 4 May 2006 with 28 votes against Fred Fono’s 22, and was sworn in. His tenure included managing recovery from riots during Rini’s premiership. On 11 October 2006, he survived a no-confidence vote with 28 votes against 17, prompted by deteriorating relations with Australia, including the expulsion of Australian High Commissioner Patrick Cole in September and the defense of suspended attorney general Julian Moti, who faces child sex charges in the Solomon Islands. On 13 October, Sogavare threatened to expel Australia from an assistance mission, and a week later, Australian peacekeepers raided his office. On 13 December 2007, he was defeated in a no-confidence vote with 25 votes in favor and 22 against, remaining in caretaker status until opposition candidate Derek Sikua was elected on 20 December 2007, when Sogavare became Leader of the Opposition. In 2010, he co-founded the Ownership, Unity and Responsibility Party, which won three seats in the 2010 general election. Following the 19 November 2014 general election, Sogavare became prime minister for the third time. On 22 September 2017, he spoke at the United Nations General Assembly, condemning North Korea’s ballistic missile tests and Indonesia’s violence in West Papua. On 7 November 2017, seventeen members of his Democratic Coalition for Change voted against him in a no-confidence motion, with Derek Sikua claiming Sogavare had lost touch with reality and fixated on conspiracy theories, while Sogavare blamed the defections on an anti-graft bill, saying some MPs feared imprisonment. Sogavare remained Acting Prime Minister until Rick Houenipwela was elected on 15 November 2017, after which he became finance minister and deputy prime minister. Shortly after the 2019 general election, Sogavare relaunched the OUR Party. On 24 April 2019, he was re-elected prime minister with more than half the vote, despite a court injunction to postpone the vote, as the Governor General, Frank Kabui, proceeded under constitutional immunity. The election triggered riots in Honiara, damaging the Pacific Casino Hotel, which Sogavare used as a campaign headquarters. On 16 September 2019, his government recognized the People's Republic of China (PRC), ending 36 years of recognition of the Republic of China, citing a bipartisan taskforce and Ministry of Foreign Affairs findings. Sogavare described the decision as a collective agreement by all Democratic Coalition Government for Advancement (DCGA) MPs. The move caused significant debate, leading to the sacking of ministers Rick Hou and Tautai Kaitu'u, with Hou claiming the decision was pre-determined. Deputy Prime Minister John Maneniaru and Education Minister Dean Kuku were also terminated, and Police Minister Lanelle Tanagada resigned. Malaita Province continued to support Taiwan and received $25 million in U.S. aid in 2020; its premier, Daniel Suidani, held an independence referendum dismissed by the national government as illegitimate. In November 2021, anti-government protesters, mostly from Malaita, burned buildings near the Parliament and looted Honiara’s Chinatown, with Sogavare resisting resignation, warning rioters would face consequences and accusing them of being politically motivated. Australia responded by deploying Federal Police and Defence Force personnel under the Australia–Solomon Islands Bilateral Security Treaty, with Papua New Guinea and Fiji also sending peacekeepers. On 6 December 2021, Sogavare survived a no-confidence motion. In 2022, he signed a wide-ranging security pact with China. The 2024 general elections were delayed from 2023 to 2024 by parliament, with Sogavare citing the country’s hosting of the Pacific Games as a reason, a move condemned by the opposition as a power grab. Sogavare led the OUR Party to win 15 seats and over 24% of the vote. On 29 April 2024, he announced he would step down as OUR Party leader and not seek re-election in the 2 May parliamentary vote, calling it a "collective decision." The Coalition of National Unity and Transformation, including Kadere and People First parties, nominated Foreign Minister Jeremiah Manele, who succeeded Sogavare as party leader and became prime minister on 2 May after defeating Matthew Wale. Sogavare was subsequently appointed finance minister. On 28 April 2025, he resigned as finance minister and joined an opposition coalition to unseat Manele, which also included Wale, Peter Kenilorea Jr., and Gordon Darcy Lilo. Manele secured enough support to avoid a no-confidence motion, and Sogavare became a backbencher for the first time since 1997. Sogavare is married to Emmy Sogavare, who owns Shadel Café, and has three children: Brandt, Shannon, and Maydrel. As prime minister, he earned a salary of 428,560 Solomon Islands dollars (approximately US$50,000). He holds a black belt in karate and is a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, having dedicated the Sogavare Memorial Seventh-day Adventist Church in memory of his father Sagavare Loko. Sogavare has been widely accused of promoting democratic backsliding, with critics describing the Solomon Islands under his leadership as increasingly autocratic or even authoritarian. Despite his modest formal salary, he has accumulated a vast real estate portfolio, raising questions about his sources of income.
